definition: Software whose source code is published under a licence that lets anyone use, study, change and redistribute it. PostgreSQL is released under the permissive PostgreSQL Licence.
example: You can download, run and modify PostgreSQL without paying a licence fee.

definition: A program that owns the stored data and answers requests from clients over a connection. It parses and runs SQL, enforces constraints, coordinates concurrent sessions and recovers after a crash.
example: Your web app, psql and a reporting tool can all connect to the same PostgreSQL database server at once.

definition: A command starting with a backslash, such as \dt or \d, that psql itself handles instead of sending it to the server as SQL. Meta-commands do not need a semicolon.
example: \dt lists tables; \d events describes the events table; \conninfo shows the current connection.

definition: In PostgreSQL, the collection of databases managed by one running server installation, sharing one data directory. It usually means a single machine, not a group of servers. Roles and some settings are cluster-wide: they belong to the whole cluster rather than one database.
example: One cluster might hold the databases postgres, postgres_study and app_prod, all served on port 5432.

definition: A named container that keeps names separate so the same name can exist in different places. In PostgreSQL a schema is a namespace inside one database, holding tables, functions and other objects.
example: public.orders and billing.orders are two different tables in two schemas of the same database.

definition: The operating-system process PostgreSQL starts to serve one client connection. It parses, plans and runs that client's SQL, sharing memory with the other backends.
example: 100 open connections normally means 100 backend processes on the server.

definition: A component that keeps a bounded set of open database connections and lends them to application requests, so each request avoids the cost of starting a new connection and backend process. It can be inside the application or a separate service such as PgBouncer.
example: A pool can reuse 20 server connections across many short application transactions; achievable throughput depends on the workload.

definition: A pooling mode in which a connection is lent to a client for one transaction only, then returned. The next transaction from the same client may use a different server connection, so session settings and temporary objects cannot be relied on.
example: With PgBouncer in transaction mode, a SET issued outside a transaction may not apply to the next query.

definition: A table or other object that lives only for the current session (or transaction) and is dropped automatically at its end. It is invisible to other sessions.
example: CREATE TEMP TABLE scratch (...) disappears when the session ends.

definition: A configured maximum number of simultaneous connections to a service. PostgreSQL's max_connections controls its client-connection cap (typically 100 by default); each connection normally needs a backend process and memory, and reserved slots reduce the capacity available to ordinary roles.
example: With max_connections set to 100, no more than 100 client connections fit. The default three superuser-reserved slots and any additional reserved_connections slots reduce the number available to an ordinary role.

definition: SQL sent with placeholders (such as $1) and the values supplied separately, so the server never interprets user input as SQL. It is the standard defence against SQL injection.
example: SELECT * FROM events WHERE id = $1, with 42 sent as the parameter.

definition: A PostgreSQL role that bypasses almost all permission checks, except the right to log in. Applications should use a non-superuser role with only the privileges they need.
example: The bootstrap role created by initdb is a superuser; its name need not be postgres.

definition: PostgreSQL’s common concept for users and groups: a named identity that can own objects and hold privileges, and can log in if it has the LOGIN attribute. Roles are cluster-wide, so pg_dump of one database does not include them.
example: CREATE ROLE shop_app LOGIN; then GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON bookings TO shop_app;

definition: A permission granted to a role on an object, such as SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE on a table. Without the privilege the operation fails.
example: GRANT SELECT ON events TO reporting grants table-read access; the role still needs applicable database and schema access, and its other grants determine what else it can do.

definition: Identifier: a value that names one row or object uniquely, often an automatically generated number. It says nothing about how many rows exist.
example: Booking ID 57 may exist alongside only 40 bookings if some inserts were rolled back.

definition: The time zone setting of the current session, used to display timestamptz values and interpret input without an offset. Changing it changes the display, not the stored instant.
example: SET TIME ZONE 'Asia/Tokyo' shows the same booking time nine hours ahead of UTC.

definition: A locking clause on SELECT that locks the returned rows so other transactions cannot update, delete or lock them until this transaction ends. It cannot lock rows that do not exist yet.
example: SELECT * FROM events WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE; holds the event row while you decide what to do.

definition: A PostgreSQL lock on a row taken by modifying or explicit row-locking statements. Conflicting writers or lockers wait, while ordinary MVCC reads can still see visible versions; different row-lock modes have different conflicts.
example: Two writers changing the same event normally wait for each other; changing different rows need not create that row-lock conflict.

definition: Informal name for a lock mode that conflicts with most or all others, above all PostgreSQL's ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, which blocks every other access to the table, including plain SELECT. VACUUM FULL and many schema changes take one.
example: While VACUUM FULL rewrites bookings, every query on bookings waits.

definition: One stored copy of a row. Under MVCC an UPDATE writes a new version and marks the old one as replaced, so concurrent snapshots can still see the version that was current for them.
example: Several updates can leave older stored copies until pruning or vacuum can reclaim them; not every version survives until a later VACUUM.

definition: An obsolete row version that is no longer visible to any snapshot the server must preserve. Its storage can be reclaimed by vacuum or, where applicable, page pruning; an old version still needed by a snapshot is not yet removable.
example: pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup is an estimate of dead row versions; it is not an exact count of distinct deleted logical rows.

definition: An isolation level in which the whole transaction sees one snapshot, taken at its first ordinary statement. It still allows write skew, and in PostgreSQL may fail with a serialization error when updating a row changed since the snapshot.
example: Repeated reads retain the same external snapshot, but also see the transaction’s own preceding changes.

definition: Running whole transactions one at a time, with no overlap. Serializable isolation promises successful concurrent transactions behave equivalently to some such order; it need not execute them physically one at a time.
example: If T1 then T2 ran serially, T2 would see that only one person was on call.

definition: A concurrency anomaly where two transactions read the same data, each makes a decision, and each writes a different row, together breaking a rule that each alone respected. Snapshot-based Repeatable Read allows it.
example: Two doctors each see two on call and each signs off: both commit, leaving none on call.

definition: Reading another transaction's uncommitted change. PostgreSQL never allows dirty reads at any isolation level.
example: A report that saw a transfer's debit before it was rolled back would have made a dirty read.

definition: A standard five-character error code returned with every SQL error, so programs can react to the kind of error rather than its message text. 40001 means serialization failure; 40P01 means deadlock detected.
example: A retry policy can restart the complete transaction on 40001 or 40P01. A 23505 unique violation needs application-specific interpretation rather than blind retry.

definition: The rules for retrying a failed operation: which errors qualify, how many attempts and how long to wait between them. Bounding it prevents endless retries under heavy contention.
example: Retry a serialization failure up to 5 times with a short random back-off, then report an error.

definition: The data structure behind an index, chosen with USING. PostgreSQL's built-in methods are B-tree (default), hash, GiST, SP-GiST, GIN and BRIN; each supports different operators.
example: CREATE INDEX ... USING gin (details) chooses the GIN method.

definition: Extra storage and work needed to keep indexes useful as rows change. Inserts generally add index entries; updates may need new entries unless optimisations such as HOT apply, and obsolete entries are reclaimed later.
example: Adding five indexes adds storage and commonly extra write work; it does not mean every UPDATE or DELETE immediately rewrites all five indexes.

definition: An index from each item inside a value (word, element, key) to the rows containing it, the reverse of storing items by row. Search engines and GIN use it.
example: For the words in 'online workshop', the index lists every row containing 'online'.

definition: Searching natural-language documents using parsed and normalised search terms rather than only exact string comparison. PostgreSQL provides configurable dictionaries, word-form normalisation and ranking functions, with tsvector and tsquery types and optional GIN indexes.
example: With PostgreSQL's English text-search configuration, a search for 'workshops' can match a document containing 'workshop'.

definition: Block Range Index: stores summaries for ranges of table pages and uses them to exclude ranges that cannot match a query. It is compact and is often effective when values correlate with physical location; candidate tuples must still be rechecked.
example: On suitably ordered timestamp data, a BRIN index can exclude page ranges outside a requested time interval.

definition: A run of consecutive PostgreSQL table pages that a BRIN index summarises as one unit. The default pages_per_range is 128; a standard-build page is 8 kB, but the build-time block size can differ.
example: With the default 128 pages per range, one BRIN entry covers about 1 MB of table.

definition: A workload dominated by adding rows rather than changing older rows. Increasing values such as timestamps may correlate with storage location, which can make BRIN useful; append-heavy alone does not guarantee physical ordering. An append-only workload specifically forbids changes to existing records.
example: An append-heavy sensor log may suit BRIN when its time values stay correlated with heap position.

definition: PostgreSQL’s ordinary table storage, with row versions in fixed-size pages and no guaranteed logical order. Index scans can use row locations to fetch heap versions; index-only scans may avoid those fetches when visibility information permits.
example: An index scan reads the B-tree, then fetches each matching row from the heap.

definition: EXPLAIN's estimate of the work a plan step needs, in arbitrary units (by default one sequential page read costs 1.0). It is for comparing plans, not a time in milliseconds.
example: cost=0.29..8.31 is a start-up cost and a total cost, both in planner units.

definition: An EXPLAIN option reporting how many pages each step found in shared buffers (hit), read from outside them (read), or dirtied and wrote. A 'read' may still come from the operating system cache.
example: Buffers: shared hit=3 read=120 means 120 pages had to be fetched from outside shared buffers.

definition: In EXPLAIN ANALYZE output, how many times a plan step was executed. Its actual time and rows are averages per loop, so multiply by loops for the total.
example: actual rows=5 loops=1000 means the step returned about 5,000 rows in total.

definition: EXPLAIN ANALYZE reports each step's time including the time of the steps beneath it, so adding parent and child times counts work twice.
example: For a simple single-loop serial Sort taking 50 ms above a 40 ms scan, subtracting gives roughly 10 ms of additional sort work. Parallel plans and loop averages need more care.

definition: PostgreSQL's own cache of table and index pages in shared memory, used by every backend. Its size is set by shared_buffers, typically 128 MB by default; a page not found there is requested from the operating system.
example: For a dedicated database server with at least 1 GB of RAM, the PostgreSQL manual suggests 25% of RAM as a starting value, followed by workload-specific measurement.

definition: Memory the operating system uses to keep recently read file data. A PostgreSQL read from outside shared buffers may be served from here without touching the disk.
example: An EXPLAIN BUFFERS read counts access outside PostgreSQL shared buffers; the OS may already have the requested file page in memory.

definition: A PostgreSQL object that supplies numbers using a configured increment, often behind identity columns. Values obtained with nextval are not reclaimed on rollback, so sequences do not guarantee gapless row IDs.
example: A rolled-back INSERT can consume an identity value; a sequence can also be configured to decrease or cycle.

definition: The PostgreSQL command that marks space held by dead row versions as reusable, updates the visibility map and freezes old transaction IDs to prevent wraparound. Plain VACUUM runs alongside normal reads and writes and rarely shrinks the file.
example: VACUUM (ANALYZE) bookings; cleans the table and refreshes its statistics.

definition: PostgreSQL’s background maintenance system that automatically schedules VACUUM and ANALYZE using activity and age criteria. It is enabled by default; trigger eligibility is not an immediate-start guarantee.
example: With PostgreSQL 18 defaults and one million estimated rows, the dead-tuple trigger threshold is 200,050; other triggers and worker availability also matter.

definition: A small per-table structure, maintained by VACUUM, recording which pages hold only rows visible to every transaction (and which are fully frozen). It lets later vacuums skip those pages and enables index-only scans.
example: An index-only scan can skip a heap fetch when the visibility map says the page is all-visible.

definition: A normal 32-bit identifier allocated when a PostgreSQL transaction or subtransaction needs one, commonly for a write. Row-version visibility uses these IDs; full 64-bit transaction IDs also include an XID epoch.
example: SELECT pg_current_xact_id(); allocates or returns a full transaction ID, including in otherwise read-only work.

definition: The visibility failure that old unfrozen committed insertions could suffer when normal 32-bit XIDs advance beyond their approximately half-range safe ordering window. Freezing protects those old insertions before they become too old for normal comparisons.
example: At exactly 1,000 allocated normal XIDs per second, two billion IDs take about 23 days; subtransactions can increase ID consumption beyond a top-level transaction rate.

definition: VACUUM’s marking of an old committed insertion as frozen so it no longer relies on normal XID age comparison. The row can still be updated or deleted later; freezing does not bypass the visibility rules for such later changes.
example: Eligible old committed insertions can be frozen; anti-wraparound vacuum advances the table’s oldest unfrozen XID boundary.

definition: A session state in which a transaction is open but no statement is running, often because the application forgot to commit. It holds locks and, if it has an old snapshot, stops vacuum removing dead rows.
example: pg_stat_activity shows state = 'idle in transaction' with a long xact_start age.

definition: A table- or index-specific setting controlling supported storage or maintenance behaviour. Tables can override some autovacuum defaults and set a fillfactor, but not every storage parameter corresponds to a server-wide setting.
example: Setting autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor to 0.01 changes the scale component to 1% of estimated table size, still subject to the base threshold and applicable cap.

definition: The fixed base added to the scale-factor component of the estimated dead-tuple trigger for autovacuum. PostgreSQL 18 defaults to 50 tuples; a separate maximum threshold can cap the result.
example: For ten estimated live rows at the default scale factor, the uncapped threshold is 52 dead versions, which may include repeated updates of the same row.

definition: The fraction of a table’s estimated row count added to the base dead-tuple threshold to decide vacuum eligibility. PostgreSQL 18 defaults to 0.2, with the result subject to the configured cap.
example: With one million estimated rows and other PostgreSQL 18 defaults, the dead-tuple trigger threshold is 200,050.

definition: A cap introduced in PostgreSQL 18 on the dead-tuple vacuum trigger threshold. It defaults to 100,000,000 tuples; setting it to -1 disables the cap.
example: With default settings and one billion estimated rows, this trigger threshold is capped at 100 million dead versions; it is not a promised start time.

definition: The allocated-XID age that a table's oldest-unfrozen-XID boundary can reach before PostgreSQL forces an anti-wraparound vacuum, even if ordinary autovacuum is disabled. The PostgreSQL 18 default is 200 million allocated transaction IDs; this is not elapsed time or a count of committed top-level transactions.
example: 200 million is under a tenth of the roughly 2.1 billion XID comparison horizon.

definition: Arithmetic on a fixed-size wrapping range, like hours on a clock. PostgreSQL uses circular comparisons of normal 32-bit XIDs, so only an approximately half-range age window is safely ordered.
example: On a 12-hour clock, 3 hours after 11 is 2.

definition: Query plan steps such as sorts, hash joins and hash aggregation that need working memory. A sort has a work_mem base allowance; hash operations use work_mem times hash_mem_multiplier, and multiple operations or parallel workers can multiply consumption.
example: A hash join followed by a sort uses working-memory plan operations; which allocations overlap and their sizes depend on the execution plan.

definition: A unit of data size. PostgreSQL memory-setting suffix GB uses 1024 MB, or 2^30 bytes; in decimal SI usage a gigabyte instead means one billion bytes.
example: 19,200 PostgreSQL MB is 18.75 PostgreSQL GB; stating the unit convention avoids ambiguity.

definition: The fixed-size block, 8 kB by default, in which PostgreSQL stores table and index data on disk and in shared buffers.
example: A 1 GB table occupies about 131,072 data pages.

definition: The property that a successfully committed change survives the failures covered by the system’s guarantees. PostgreSQL normally waits for local WAL durability, but asynchronous commit and unsafe storage settings weaken this guarantee.
example: With synchronous_commit = off, the last fraction of a second of commits can be lost in a crash.

definition: Making buffered writes durable on storage under the configured storage guarantees. PostgreSQL normally flushes commit WAL before acknowledging a transaction, but asynchronous commit can acknowledge earlier.
example: With synchronous_commit = off, a crash can lose recent acknowledged transactions even though database consistency is preserved.

definition: A commit acknowledgement that waits for the configured persistence or replica conditions before returning. PostgreSQL's synchronous_commit setting selects local WAL and optional standby waits: on normally waits for local WAL flush and any configured synchronous-standby feedback, while off can return before local WAL flush.
example: SET synchronous_commit = off speeds commits but risks losing the most recent ones in a crash.

definition: A PostgreSQL recovery reference point associated with writing dirty pages and recording checkpoint information in WAL. Recovery starts from its recorded redo position, which can precede checkpoint completion; a checkpoint is not a backup.
example: PostgreSQL 18 checkpoint_timeout defaults to five minutes between automatic checkpoints; WAL volume can trigger one sooner, while checkpoint work takes time.

definition: PostgreSQL’s replay of WAL from the checkpoint’s redo position after an unclean stop to restore a consistent state. With normal durability settings it retains durable committed changes, including accidental but valid writes.
example: Crash recovery cannot decide that an acknowledged DELETE was a user mistake.

definition: PostgreSQL's built-in replication: the primary server streams WAL records to standby servers as they are generated, and the standbys replay them to stay a copy of the primary.
example: primary_conninfo on a standby tells it which primary server to connect to and stream WAL from.

definition: A server that continuously applies the primary's WAL. It can take over on failover and, as a hot standby, serve read-only queries.
example: A reporting query can run on a hot standby to keep load off the primary.

definition: The server that accepts writes and sends its WAL to standbys.
example: All bookings are written on the primary server; standbys only replay its changes.

definition: A copy of a database kept up to date from another server; in PostgreSQL usually a standby fed by streaming replication.
example: A read replica in another data centre can serve queries; promotion and acceptable failover data loss require an explicit operational plan.

definition: Replication where the primary can acknowledge a commit without waiting for a standby acknowledgement. Standbys can lag, and failover can lose acknowledged commits that the promoted standby has not received.
example: A standby 2 seconds behind can lose 2 seconds of commits if it is promoted after the primary dies.

definition: Replication where COMMIT waits until a configured standby confirms it has the WAL (and, depending on settings, flushed or replayed it). It reduces failover data loss at the cost of latency and availability.
example: synchronous_commit = remote_apply waits until the standby has replayed the commit.

definition: How far a standby is behind the primary, in time or WAL bytes. Reads from a lagging standby see older data.
example: pg_stat_replication reports acknowledgement delays such as replay_lag; these are not predictions of how long a standby will take to catch up.

definition: Applying WAL records to data pages to redo changes, during crash recovery, on a standby or when restoring a backup.
example: Point-in-time recovery replays archived WAL up to a chosen timestamp.

definition: Switching service from a failed primary to a standby, which is promoted to become the new primary. With asynchronous replication, commits the standby had not received are lost.
example: pg_ctl promote turns a standby into a writable primary.

definition: Turning a standby into a primary that accepts writes, usually during failover.
example: SELECT pg_promote(); promotes the standby it runs on.

definition: The guarantee that a user who has just written data sees their write on their next read. Reading from an asynchronous standby can break it.
example: After a confirmed commit, route a freshness-sensitive read to the primary or wait for the chosen standby to replay the required WAL; a fixed delay alone is no guarantee.

definition: PostgreSQL's tool for a logical backup of one database: SQL or an archive that recreates its objects and data. It does not include roles or other cluster-wide objects; pg_dumpall covers those.
example: pg_dump -Fc shop > shop.dump, restored with pg_restore.

definition: A physical copy of a PostgreSQL cluster's data files. pg_basebackup can produce one while the server runs; together with the WAL needed to make it consistent and reach a target, a suitable base backup is the starting point for point-in-time recovery.
example: pg_basebackup -D /backups/base copies the data directory from a running server.

definition: Retaining completed WAL segment files in separate storage. A suitable base backup and an unbroken required WAL sequence support recovery to a reachable target; archive delays and missing segments affect recoverability.
example: The default WAL segment size is 16 MB, but initdb can choose a different segment size.

definition: Restoring a suitable physical base backup and replaying the required continuous WAL to a configured target, such as a timestamp. The target must be after the base backup finished; inclusive/exclusive target settings determine which boundary transaction is included.
example: Recover to 14:02:59 to get back the rows deleted at 14:03.

definition: The maximum amount of recent work, measured in time, that you accept losing in a disaster. It drives backup frequency, WAL archiving and replication choices.
example: A five-minute RPO requires a design that limits recoverable-data loss to five minutes; merely scheduling a backup job is not proof of that limit.

definition: The maximum downtime you accept before service is restored after a failure. Measure it with real test restores.
example: Restoring a 2 TB backup in 6 hours fails an RTO of 1 hour.

definition: A database service operated by a provider that automates selected tasks such as backups and patching. Failover features and guarantees depend on the chosen deployment; the user still needs to understand retention, recovery and availability limits.
example: As documented in October 2026, Amazon RDS DB instances allow automated-backup retention from 0 to 35 days; DB clusters have different limits and support depends on the deployment.

definition: A system view with one row per server process, showing its current query, state (such as active or idle in transaction) and what it is waiting for.
example: SELECT pid, state, wait_event FROM pg_stat_activity; shows process state and waits, which must be interpreted to diagnose blocking.

definition: A system view of outstanding server lock requests, including held and awaited locks. Row-lock ownership is normally recorded on disk rather than listed directly here; a session waiting on a row often appears as waiting for the holder’s transaction ID. Use pg_blocking_pids with pg_stat_activity to investigate blockers.
example: SELECT pg_blocking_pids(1234); lists the sessions blocking process 1234.

definition: The name in a name-value pair of a JSON object, such as "format" in {"format":"online"}. JSONB keeps only the last value when a key is repeated and does not keep the input order of keys.
example: '{"a":1,"a":2}'::jsonb is stored as {"a": 2}.

definition: A change to the structure of the database, such as ALTER TABLE adding a column or CREATE INDEX, made with DDL statements. Many take locks that conflict with ordinary reads or writes on the table.
example: ALTER TABLE bookings ADD COLUMN note text; takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE in this ordinary case, and acquiring the lock can wait behind long-running transactions.

definition: A configured stopping target for PostgreSQL recovery, such as a time, transaction ID, WAL position or named restore point. The target and inclusive/exclusive settings determine what is replayed; choosing a target before a mistake can recover earlier state.
example: recovery_target_time = '2027-05-01 14:02:59+00' stops replay one second before a 14:03 deletion.

definition: The reproducible example schema in this PostgreSQL module: an events table with seats_left and a bookings table with a unique request_key and an event foreign key. Use a fresh disposable database for independent write experiments.
example: The first inserted workshop has two seats; later examples either continue that setup or explicitly reset their starting state.

definition: The normal PostgreSQL transaction identifier recorded in row-version headers. Its 32-bit representation has a circular ordering window of approximately two billion allocated IDs; freezing protects old committed insertions from aging beyond that window.
example: Full transaction IDs returned as xid8 include additional XID epoch information, unlike the normal row-header XID.

definition: A PostgreSQL vacuum forced by transaction-ID or multixact aging to advance safe visibility horizons. It can run even when ordinary autovacuum is disabled, and old retained snapshots or other blockers may prevent enough progress.
example: The PostgreSQL 18 autovacuum_freeze_max_age default is 200 million allocated transaction IDs.

definition: The higher-order counter included with a normal 32-bit PostgreSQL transaction ID in a full transaction ID. It tracks wraparounds, allowing xid8 values to represent the longer-running sequence rather than only the repeating low 32 bits.
example: pg_current_xact_id() returns the full xid8 representation, while ordinary row headers hold a normal XID.

definition: A named namespace inside one PostgreSQL database, containing objects such as tables, types and functions. Different schemas can contain objects with the same name; privileges govern access. This is distinct from the general use of schema to mean the design of a database.
example: public.orders and billing.orders identify two separate tables in two schemas of the same database.

definition: A PostgreSQL role without the SUPERUSER attribute. It is subject to normal privilege checks, but its granted privileges and other role attributes still determine its powers; lacking SUPERUSER alone does not make it least-privileged.
example: An application role should lack SUPERUSER and receive only the database, schema, table and sequence privileges its operations require.
